articles.title: UAW Members Voting for International Officers
articles.author: Detroit DSA
articles.content_excerpt: Delegates to the UAW Convention in June heard candidates for top offices. Any active member could run; there was no signature-gathering requirement as in some other unions. Photo: Jim West | jimwestphoto.com By Luis Feliz Leon and Jane Slaughter United Auto Workers members are voting by mail ballot for their top officers, for the second time in the union’s 91 years. Ballots went out August 21 and are due back by October 5. The contest will decide whether President Shawn Fain, who became famous for leading 2023’s Stand-Up Strike against the Big 3 automakers, will be able to continue the union’s about-face from its previous employer-friendly ways. articles.title: Colombia’s Far Right Sees an Earthquake as an Opportunity
articles.author: Cruz Bonlarron Martínez
articles.content_excerpt: On August 10, western Colombia was rocked by a 7.8 magnitude earthquake. Images of collapsed buildings and ordinary citizens organizing to remove the rubble quickly circulated on social media and through news agencies. Cali, the region’s largest city, quickly became the week’s trending topic. This came just three days after the country’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella had taken power in a highly divisive and militarized spectacle held at a military base in the city, which voted overwhelmingly for his leftist competitor Iván Cepeda. Now after the earthquake, Cali and western Colombia are taking center stage in the administration’s reversal of Gustavo Petro’s redistributive policies and its attempt to refound Colombia as a bastion of far-right politics. articles.title: James Lawson Was the Civil Rights Movement’s Drill Sergeant
articles.author: Chris Maisano
articles.content_excerpt: Reverend James Lawson Jr did not attend the 1963 March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. Most of the movement’s boldfaced names — the “Big Six” civil rights leaders, labor leaders and religious figures, celebrities and entertainers — were there, in front of a quarter million people up on the Lincoln Memorial’s marble steps. But Lawson was not. He was hundreds of miles away from the nation’s capital, organizing and training people at a regional gathering of Methodist student leaders in Upstate New York. Lawson and his colleagues paused the proceedings so that anyone who wanted to board a bus to Washington early that morning could do so. “I had planned to go,” recalls Lawson in his landmark memoir, Nonviolent , “but we didn’t have enough room for every student who wanted to attend. articles.title: The Customer Is Always Watching
articles.author: Alex N. Press
articles.content_excerpt: Toru Hinkle was stocking shelves at Target when two customers appeared. Toru asked if they needed help. The men wanted a price check on an item that cost $20, but even after Hinkle told them the price, they kept asking. Eventually Hinkle noticed a blinking light on one customer’s glasses. Mia Sato reported what happened next for The Verge , speaking with Hinkle and other workers about the new problems posed by customers wearing Ray-Ban Meta glasses. The men were filming Hinkle. They kept up the bit, repeatedly asking the price and deliberately misgendering Hinkle (who uses “they/them” pronouns) and a manager who came over to help. articles.title: Trump’s Art of the Bad Deal Comes to Canada
articles.author: Stuart Trew
articles.content_excerpt: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s decision to withdraw his trade negotiating team from Washington last Friday was surprising and refreshing. Surprising because Carney clearly wanted a deal and has a record of conceding to Donald Trump again and again , to no effect, in hopes of securing one. Refreshing because the deal on offer would have been terrible for Canadian workers. The interests of labor and capital are not the same, and Carney’s position is not the Left’s. Canadian workers care about the health of their country’s productive base but have no interest in undercutting American workers in this trade war, which is doing the latter no favors in any case. articles.title: France Needs a President Who Isn’t for the Bosses
articles.author: Marlon Ettinger
articles.content_excerpt: Heavy rain pummeled the canopy over the covered stage in Paris’s Roland-Garros stadium on Thursday night, midway through the first debate for next spring’s French presidential election. The seven candidates present, who included Jean-Luc Mélenchon, Marine Le Pen, Édouard Philippe, Gabriel Attal, Raphaël Glucksmann, and Marine Tondelier, volleyed competing economic visions in front of a buttoned-up crowd of entrepreneurs and business leaders attending the Movement of French Businesses’ (Medef) summer conference. There was plenty on stage for Medef corporate chiefs to cheer for. The pro-business, deregulation-happy employers’ union has already enjoyed a long string of political wins since its founding in 1998. articles.title: Review: The Wind Cries Freedom: An Oral History of the Next American Revolution
articles.author: Detroit DSA
articles.content_excerpt: The cover for The Wind Cries Freedom by Michael Albert By Will Froberg Michael Albert takes you into a parallel universe in which the fictional Revolutionary Participatory Society (RPS) mass movement has grasped the levers of power in the United States, and is now in the process of implementing their participatory vision. Through a series of interviews with RPS organizers, Albert explains the means by which the movement eventually prevailed. Their vision includes an alternative to capitalism called a participatory economy , which the author invented alongside Robin Hahnel back in the 1960’s, and which he has spent his life advocating for.
